preface.title: Preface
preface.text: They pushed it to the end of the alphabet, into the corners of maps, to the foot of letters we dare not finish. They gave it all they could not name: the unknown, the treasure, the light that passes through hands, the names of those who could not write their own. It carried everything without a word. Two strokes, nothing more. This book is for it. To honour it, most of these pages are written in its own tongue, the X language. Do not try to translate it. It says nothing, and it says everything. Read it the way you listen to rain.

chapters.title: Before Letters
chapters.text: Long before alphabets, there were already two strokes that cross. In a cave by the sea, at the southern tip of Africa, someone scratched them into a piece of ochre more than seventy thousand years ago. They turn up on bones, on stones, deep in caves. No one knows what they meant. A count, perhaps. A name. A place to come back to. Those who drew them left without another word. Only the sign remains, and the sign is still waiting for xxxxxxx xx xxxx.

chapters.title: Chi
chapters.text: The Greeks called it chi, and said it from the back of the throat, like a rasping breath. But not all Greeks wrote alike. In the East it was read “kh”. In the West, on Euboea, it was read “ks”. Sailors from Euboea put to sea and founded Cumae, on the coast of Italy. They took their letters with them. The Etruscans took the letters from them, and the Latins from the Etruscans. That is how the western X, the one that says “ks”, crossed the sea and settled xxxx xxx xxxx.

chapters.title: Ten
chapters.text: In Rome, the X began to count. Ten. Some say it is two Vs, two open hands, one upon the other. Others say it is the stroke drawn across the tally, every tenth notch. No one is sure. For a long time it was the last letter of the Latin alphabet. After it, there was nothing. Then, in the first century before our era, Y and Z were brought from Greece to write Greek words. They were put behind it. It was no longer the last. It never xxxxx xxxxxxxx.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.text: For centuries, most people could not write. So at the foot of contracts, marriage records, baptismal registers, someone handed them the pen, and they drew a cross. The clerk wrote the name around it: “the mark of John”, “the mark of Mary”. Millions of lives fit into those two strokes, all alike, and yet each one trembled in its own way. The X signed for everyone. It never signed for itself. Its own name, xx xxxxx xxxx.

chapters.title: The Kiss
chapters.text: No one quite knows when it began. It is said that long ago, the cross at the foot of a letter was an oath, kissed to make it sacred. Then the oath went away, and the kiss stayed. Today, at the end of messages, there is one, then two, then three. Xxx. We add them without thinking, to say goodbye, to say see you soon, to say what we do not write. The X keeps all those kisses. It never xxxxx xxxx. Xxx xxxxx.

chapters.title: The Unknown
chapters.text: In 1637, Descartes published La Géométrie. In it he named a, b, c the quantities we know, and x, y, z those we seek. They say the printer, short of type, had more x’s than other letters in his cases, and chose them. It is probably untrue, but the story is too lovely to forget. Since then, X is what we do not know. What must be found. We isolate it, surround it, push it to one side of the equals sign. And when at last we find it, it stops being an X. It xxxxxxx x xxxxxx.

chapters.title: Times
chapters.text: In 1631, an English country parson, William Oughtred, tipped the X onto its side and made it a sign: ×. From then on, it would multiply. Two times two, ten times over, a thousand times thank you. Not everyone liked it. Leibniz wrote that it was too easily mistaken for the letter, and that a simple dot would do better. The dot found its followers. The × kept its own. It stayed, leaning a little, between the numbers, making everything it touches grow, xxxx xxxxxx xxxxxxx.

chapters.title: The Treasure
chapters.text: On the map in Treasure Island, Stevenson drew three red crosses. Since then, X marks the spot. You count your steps from the tall tree, turn your back to the hill, dig beneath the cross. Treasure maps are full of Xs, and beaches full of holes. Most of the time, there is nothing. But we dig anyway, because someone, one day, took the trouble to draw the cross. Those who drew it never come back. They xxxxxxx xxx xxxxxx.

chapters.title: The Rays
chapters.text: On 8 November 1895, in Würzburg, Wilhelm Röntgen saw a screen glow in the dark of his laboratory. A light was passing through cardboard, wood, flesh. A few weeks later he photographed his wife’s hand: the bones, and the ring around them. It is said that when she saw it, she whispered: “I have seen my death.” Röntgen did not know what this light was. So he called it X, like the unknown. The name stayed, even once it was known. The X sees through everything, xxxx xx xxxx xxxxxx.

chapters.title: Quixote
chapters.text: In old Spanish, X said neither “ks” nor “kh”. It hushed: “sh”. People wrote Don Quixote, and English still writes him so. Then the language changed. The “sh” hardened into the rasping sound heard in “jota”, and in 1815 the Academy decided to write it J. Quixote became Quijote. But Mexico refused. México kept its X, and Oaxaca, and Texas. The knight, in Spain, lost his letter along the way. Xx xxxxxxx xxxx xx.

chapters.title: The Box
chapters.text: In many countries, people vote with a cross. Just one, in the right box, in pencil, behind a curtain. No one must know who drew it. It is anonymous, and that is what keeps it safe. Misplaced, one stroke too long, and it spoils everything. Well placed, added to millions of others, it changes a country. Two strokes, always the same, and behind each one, someone who hesitated. The X decides without ever xxxxxx xx xxx.

chapters.title: In the Library
chapters.text: Here, every book holds Xs. They are everywhere, in the middle of words that mean nothing, at the ends of lines, at the tops of pages. Some books hold only one, and others none at all. This one is made of nothing else. Page after page, line after line, nothing but it. The X believes it is alone. It always has. It does not look closely. Xx xx xxxx xxx xxx xxxxx.

deathBook.name: The DeathBook
rules: The reader whose name is written in this notebook shall never leave the Library.
The notebook takes effect only if the writer has seen the reader's face. The mirror of a vestibule will do.
A written name cannot be erased. A copy already exists, one letter apart, in another hexagon.
There is no use looking for the way out in the books: all of them describe it, none of them contains it.
Every name written here is that of a reader the Library has kept.
The notebook never runs out of pages. There is always one left for the next name.
If the circumstances are written after the name, they shall come to pass.
circumstances: hexagon 4021, while reading
on the stairs, between two galleries
at the foot of a shelf, a book open over the face
searching for the catalogue of catalogues
before the mirror of the vestibule
at the end of an unlit gallery
counting the books on the fifth shelf
on the last page
leaning over the railing, without falling
copying out a page that made no sense
closing a book too soon
on the landing, not knowing whether going up or down
in the air shaft, between two floors
looking for a book about oneself
after reading the same page a thousand times
by the light of the last lamp
waiting for someone who never came
deciphering a line that made sense
in the closet, standing, to sleep
in the middle of a sentence
putting a book back in its place
without finding what was sought
believing what was sought had been found
the day the counting of hexagons stopped
between two books identical but for a comma
writing one's own name
listening to footsteps, overhead
following a gallery that turned back on itself
after the thousandth crossing
scenario: {name} takes a book from the Library.
Reads it to the last page.
The last page closes nothing: it opens a door.
Takes another. Then another. Then another still.
The end of a book is only the threshold of the next.
And every beginning promises an end it does not always keep.

oriana.name: The Biography of Oriana
oriana.subtitle: One Block at a Time
quotes: “She explained blockchain to me between Lisbon and Madrid.”
“She closed the bar, then explained blockchain to me.”
oriana.blurb: Developer, traveller, queen of late nights and apostle of the blockchain: Oriana has a story to tell. Several, actually. All at once. From her first word to the suitcase packed for America, the life of a woman who never kept it short, told by a biographer who tried.
copyright: © Oriana. All rights reserved, all blocks validated.
in the writing of this book.
Excessive anecdotes may harm the health
of those around you. Read responsibly.
dedication: who listened to me talk about blockchain

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: The First Word
opening: Oriana’s first word was not “mummy”. Nor “daddy”. According to her mother, it was a full sentence, with a subordinate clause, spoken at eleven months to a baker who hadn’t asked for anything.¹ She hasn’t really stopped for breath since.
At school, her reports all said the same thing, in different handwriting: “Brilliant pupil. Talkative.” One maths teacher once added: “Very talkative. But she’s right.” She had it framed.
This book tells her life. It could have been shorter. She asked to proofread it.
chapters.note: It was a question. And the baker answered.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: Developer
opening: Oriana became a developer by accident, one evening when she was explaining to a friend why his website didn’t work. By midnight, the website worked. By one, the friend was asleep. She was still talking.¹

At work, she is one of those people who ask questions in meetings, then answer them. “Any questions? — No. — I’ll answer anyway.” Her colleagues find her brilliant, funny and sometimes a little tiring, but always in that order.
She codes fast and well, with music on and a cup of tea going cold. Her commit messages are short. It is, by general agreement, the only short thing about her.
chapters.note: He wasn’t asleep, he was thinking. I checked by asking him the question again the next day.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: The Revelation
opening: She discovered blockchain on a Tuesday, in an article nobody had recommended. By the end of the first page, she understood. By the end of the second, she was convinced. By the end of the third, she was already explaining it to the colleague at the next desk, who was on the phone.¹

A ledger nobody can erase, where every block remembers the one before: for someone who never forgets anything anyone has told her, it was almost obvious. That evening she told anyone who would listen: “It’s me, as a technology.”
Nobody argued. Nobody argues with Oriana for very long.
chapters.note: He hung up. So he was interested.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: The Gospel
opening: Ever since, she has been explaining blockchain. To her colleagues, her family, the baker, the bus driver, strangers on a night train who hadn’t asked for anything and who, by morning, knew what proof of stake is.¹
She has a short version, twenty minutes long, and a long version nobody has ever heard in full. She always starts with: “Picture a big notebook.” You never know when she’ll stop. Neither does she.
Rumour has it that the baker eventually bought a token. She refuses to talk about it. Oriana talks about it a lot.
chapters.note: “Who hadn’t asked for anything”: that’s the biographer talking. I saw their eyes. They were asking.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Around the World
opening: Oriana took her first plane at nineteen. By landing, she knew the first names, jobs and holiday plans of both her neighbours in the row, and the flight attendant’s too.¹ Since then, she has never really travelled alone: there is always someone next to her, and they always end up listening.

Lisbon, Tokyo, Reykjavik, Marrakech: she collects stamps in her passport and conversations in taxis. They say a driver in Lisbon went round the city twice just to hear the end of her explanation of proof of work.
She comes back from every trip with too many photos, too many stories and not enough time to tell them all. She tries anyway. The notebook that follows gives an idea, in shorter form.
chapters.note: And the pilot’s. He came to say hello at the end; we talked for half an hour on the jet bridge.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: Last Orders
opening: Oriana loves parties. The long ones, the ones that start with “just one drink” and end when the bar closes, or a little after. She is always the last to leave, because there is always someone she hasn’t talked to yet.¹

At three in the morning, you’ll usually find her by the decks, explaining blockchain to the DJ. He nods along to the beat. She takes it as a yes. The mornings after are hard, but her memories are intact: she can tell you who said what, and at what time.
Nobody remembers how those nights end. The blockchain does. So does Oriana.
chapters.note: I wasn’t drunk, I was enthusiastic.

chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: The Five-Minute Meeting
opening: The meeting was meant to last five minutes. It said so in the invitation, in bold: “quick sync”. Oriana had just one remark. She raised her hand at 10:01.¹

By 10:20, she had reached the remark, or at least its background. By 10:40, she had answered three questions nobody had asked. At 11:00, someone opened the window. At 11:02, she concluded: “Anyway, that’s all.” It was not all.
Since then, the team always books an hour for quick syncs. They often finish early. Except when Oriana has a remark.
chapters.note: The remark was important, and so was the rest. Besides, nobody left. Well, one colleague, but he had a train to catch. I sent him the end in writing. Four pages. He thanked me. Well, he gave it a thumbs-up.

chapters.label: Chapter 8
chapters.title: The Cat on the Keyboard
opening: Oriana has cats. They listen to her talk about blockchain without ever interrupting, which makes them, in her opinion, the best colleagues she has ever had.¹

One of them likes to sleep on her keyboard. One day, it pushed a commit: “ggggggggggggggg”. AlexH, her colleague, reviewed it with the utmost seriousness. He left a single comment: “Rename.” Oriana defended the cat for twenty minutes. The commit is still there.
This is the shortest chapter in the book. She found it too short. The cat said nothing.
chapters.note: That’s also why I talk to them so much. Somebody has to talk in this house. They have opinions, mind you, but they keep them to themselves, which I respect, even if I don’t understand it.

chapters.label: Chapter 9
chapters.title: America
opening: Oriana dreams of living in the United States. She talks about it often, mostly New York, sometimes Austin, once Seattle “for the rain”. She has even started her visa application. It is almost ready.¹

She has it all planned: the apartment with a view, the corner café where she’ll know everyone within a week, and the first American she’ll explain blockchain to. He doesn’t know it yet. He has a few months of peace left.
The suitcase is half packed, in a corner of the bedroom. The cat sleeps in it.
chapters.note: “Almost” meaning two documents are missing, well, three, and an ID photo where I’m not talking, which is harder than you’d think: the photographer tried four times, the fifth was the one but my eyes were closed, he said it would do, I don’t think so, nor does the embassy, so I’m going back on Tuesday.

chapters.title: Epilogue: Anyway
opening: This book ends here. Oriana doesn’t. As you read these lines, she is surely telling someone something, in great detail, with a parenthesis that will never close.¹

One day, she will move to the other side of the ocean. She will look at the city from her window, coffee in hand, and call the friends she left behind to tell them everything. The call will be long. They will pick up anyway.
She said she’d keep it short. She said “anyway”. We believe her.

oriana.longLine: She has long dreamt of living in the United States.¹
oriana.longNote: “Long” is a figure of speech, we should be precise: since 2009 exactly, since a documentary about San Francisco I watched at my aunt’s, the one with the ginger cat, not the other one. Besides, it isn’t a dream, it’s a plan, and a plan isn’t a dream because it has steps. Step one: the application. New York for the energy, Austin for tech, Seattle for the rain that will remind me of home, but not too much. oriana.journalIntro: Oriana writes everything down. Since she discovered blockchain, she writes it in blocks: each block keeps the fingerprint of the one before, and nothing is ever erased. Here are the latest. There are more.
oriana.thanks: Thank you to everyone who listened to me: my colleagues, my friends, my cats, Rui, the DJ in Montreal, the karaoke man and the United States embassy, which will listen to me soon. Thank you to AlexH, who proofread this book and requested changes on every footnote. Thank you to the biographer, who did his best to cut me off and almost never managed. And thank you, reader: if you want to know more, come and see me. I have time.

alexH.name: AlexH, My Code, My PR
quotes: “Finally, a flawless book: he reviewed himself.”
alexH.blurb: From the first “Hello, world” to his ten-thousandth change request, the life of a lead dev who lets nothing slide: not a variable name, not a comma, not a line too long. The bugs got through anyway.
copyright: No tests were harmed in the writing of this book.
The bugs described are real; any resemblance to
dedication: the only one stricter than me.

chapters.title: Prologue
opening: It all starts with a comma. The one missing, one morning, from a sticky note on the office fridge: “Milk, coffee sugar”. He added it in pen, between “coffee” and “sugar”, without a word to anyone. Nobody had asked him to. Nobody thanked him.

That was his first review. Ten thousand more would follow, all just as precise, all just as unsolicited. Variable names, lines too long, trailing spaces nobody else could see. He could see them. He still does.
This book tells that life, PR by PR. It has been proofread, of course. Several times. By him. You will not find a single typo in it. As for bugs, we guarantee nothing.

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: Hello, World
opening: His first program was one line long. It printed “Hello, world” and worked on the first try, which should have been enough. He rewrote it four times that evening anyway. The quotes were the wrong kind. The indentation was off by one space. And “world”, in his view, deserved an explanation.
The fifth version was eleven lines long. It was commented, typed, filed in a folder with his name on it. It printed “Hello, world” exactly like the first one, but with a clear conscience.

That evening he understood something essential: a program that works is only a draft. A clean program, on the other hand, is a work of art. Whether it works is a detail to be sorted out later, usually in another ticket.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: First Commit
opening: The message of his first commit was three paragraphs long. The first explained why. The second explained how. The third announced what he planned to do next, with a date. He was already following, without knowing it, a convention that did not exist yet.

The code itself was two lines. One fixed a typo in a comment. Nobody ever found out what the other one did. He discovered it six years later, rereading his history one Sunday, for fun. He opened a ticket against himself. He rejected it: the title was badly worded.

Since then he commits often, and always well. Every message starts with an imperative verb. None says “wip”. None says “fix”. There is one, just one, that says “oops”. He claims it wasn’t him. Git blame claims otherwise.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: The Conflict
opening: The conflict came on a Thursday, around 3 pm. Two branches, one file, two worldviews: one indented with tabs, the other with spaces. The whole team gathered around his screen. Some were already talking about a holy war.

He settled it in ten seconds. Spaces, two per level, as it should be. He then reread the file’s four hundred lines, renamed three functions along the way and put the imports back in order. The merge was gorgeous.
The rest of the conflict, something about a dropped database table, waited until Monday. Nobody had noticed. To be fair, the code that dropped it was remarkably well written.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: The Review
opening: To him, a review is not a formality. It is a conversation, long, precise and usually one-way. He reads every line. He comments on every name. He asks why. Then he asks why again, in case the first answer was just an excuse.

Legend has it that a three-line PR once got forty-two comments from him. Not true: there were forty-three, but the last one simply said “thanks”. Those who survived his reviews speak of them with respect, and a slight weariness. All of them write flawless code today.

And when the PR finally goes through, clean as a whistle, sometimes the bug is still in it. But it is well named, properly typed, and documented. Just read the comment above it: “TODO: check this case”. Spelled perfectly.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Friday, 5:59 pm
opening: He had said it, and even written it in the README: no deploys on Fridays. The rule was in bold, with an example and a counterexample. Nobody could claim not to know it.

That Friday, the PR was perfect. Reviewed, formatted, every variable carefully named, not a comma out of place. He had approved it at 5:40 pm, adding: “for Monday”. At 5:59 pm, someone clicked the button. At 6:02 pm, production went down.

He spent the evening putting things right, calmly, without a word of reproach. The error message, at least, was perfectly indented. He pointed it out on Monday morning, in the meeting. It was the only positive thing he said that day.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: Rollback
opening: Going back is not a failure, he likes to say. It is a commit like any other, as long as it is well written. That evening he undid three days of work in a single command, without flinching.

Then he spent an hour on the rollback’s message. It explained what had been done, why it had to be undone, and how to keep it from happening again. The text was so clear, so well structured, that it now hangs in the break room.
The bug, however, never left. It was in another file, one the rollback hadn’t touched. It is still there. But next to it, these days, everything is very clean.

chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: Refactor
opening: Nobody had asked him for a refactor. He did one anyway, on a Sunday, “just to rename two or three things”. On Monday the PR touched three hundred files. Nothing was called what it used to be.

Everything was clearer. Functions finally said what they did. Folders were sorted logically, then alphabetically. The tests, all three of them, had been renamed too. They all failed, but under perfectly explicit names.
He judged it a good start. The team took two weeks to find their files again. None had been changed, except for their names. To this day, it is the best-named refactor in the project’s history.

chapters.title: Epilogue: LGTM
opening: Today he still reviews. PRs, READMEs, his colleagues’ messages, restaurant menus and road signs. He once wrote to a town hall about a comma. He won.

Only once in his career did he type “LGTM” and nothing else. People still talk about it in hushed voices, by the coffee machine. Some say he was tired. Others that he hadn’t read it. He maintains the code was simply perfect.
This book ends here, but his reviews don’t. If you find a mistake in it, open a ticket: he will read it. If there is a bug, on the other hand, don’t worry. It is surely very well named.

blurb: Banners, countdowns, pre-ticked boxes: ten patterns that keep the reader in, taken apart one by one.

prefaceText: People often ask me what separates a good interface from an effective one. The answer fits in one sentence: a good interface lets you leave.

For years, I watched teams measure their success by the time users could not manage to lose. A paler button, a box already ticked, a countdown that never ends. Each of these choices is small. Together, they draw a room with no door.

This book shows them all. It does not recommend them. Sylvain and Aymeric F. took them apart one by one, with the patience of those who watched them being born, so that we learn to recognise them: we only protect ourselves well from what we can name.
prefaceMore: I have only one piece of advice for the reader: read it to the end. Not because you will be forced to, but because on the last page, you will know where the exits are.
howToText: Each chapter presents a pattern in three steps: the pattern, why it works, an example.
All the examples are interactive. They behave exactly as they do on the web.
Don't worry. You will always be able to turn the page.

chapters.name: Informed consent
chapters.motif: A banner covers the page. A big coloured button offers to accept everything. Refusing exists too, but further away: behind “Settings”, at the end of a list of boxes already ticked.
chapters.why: The reader came to read, not to configure. Every extra click is a price. Nothing is forbidden: refusing simply costs more.
chapters.keep: The choice is free. It is just further away.
chapters.exercise: Find the “Reject” button on this page.

chapters.name: The shy button
chapters.motif: The button that lets you leave exists. It is even clearly visible. It just happens not to like being approached.
chapters.why: Nobody chases a button for long. After a few seconds, most readers decide they did not really want to leave.
chapters.keep: An exit you cannot reach is as good as no exit, and costs less.
chapters.exercise: Touch the word “exit” at the bottom of this page.

chapters.name: Caring urgency
chapters.motif: A countdown, a dwindling stock. Then, for whoever refuses, a sentence to click that makes them look foolish: “No thanks, I'd rather stay ignorant.”
chapters.why: Fear of missing out pushes people to decide fast. Shame stops them from saying no. Together, they leave almost no room for thought.
chapters.keep: The countdown does not need to end. It needs to be seen.
chapters.exercise: You have ten seconds to read this sentence. Or nine.

chapters.name: Loyalty
chapters.motif: Subscribing takes one click. Unsubscribing takes a journey: a confirmation, a second one, a survey, then a question phrased so that you no longer know what you are answering.
chapters.why: At each step, some readers give up. Those who reach the end are rare, and they have earned the right to leave.
chapters.keep: A front door, a maze for an exit.
chapters.exercise: Cross out whichever does not apply: I stay / I stay.

chapters.name: The premium offer
chapters.motif: To continue, you must choose a plan. All of them cost something; the most expensive one is highlighted. The free version exists, in very small print, under a discouraging word: “not recommended”.
chapters.why: A choice between three prices is no longer a choice between paying or not. The reader compares, and forgets they could take nothing.
chapters.keep: Never ask “do you want one?”. Ask “which one?”.
chapters.exercise: How much does the free version cost? Explain.

chapters.name: The thoughtful basket
chapters.motif: At checkout, the basket holds one more item: insurance, a donation, a second copy. The box was ticked. You only had to see it.
chapters.why: Removing takes effort and a little nerve. Keeping takes nothing.
chapters.keep: What the reader did not refuse, they wanted.
chapters.exercise: Without looking: how many items are in your basket?

chapters.name: Discreet advertising
chapters.motif: The ad takes the shape of the content: same font, same place, and a big “Download” button that is not the right one.
chapters.why: The eye looks for a shape, not a label.
chapters.keep: The best ad placement is wherever the reader was about to click.
chapters.exercise: This exercise is brought to you by our partners.

chapters.name: Social proof
chapters.motif: “12 people are reading this page right now.” “A reader from the next hexagon has just finished it.” Nobody checks.
chapters.why: What others do seems safe. What others are doing right now seems urgent.
chapters.keep: A crowd is drawn faster than it gathers.
chapters.exercise: 1,247 readers passed this exercise. Will you?

chapters.name: The well-phrased question
chapters.motif: “Untick this box if you do not wish not to receive our offers.” The sentence is correct. It is simply not meant to be understood.
chapters.why: Faced with a difficult sentence, people leave the box as it is.
chapters.keep: A reader in a hurry keeps what was ticked for them.
chapters.exercise: Do not tick this box if you do not want not to tick it.

chapters.name: The endless scroll
chapters.motif: There is no bottom of the page. When readers think they have reached the end, more pages appear.
chapters.why: Without an end, there is never a good moment to stop.
chapters.keep: A book that ends is a book you close.

rabbit.name: The Wild Rabbit
title: THE WILD
RABBIT
rabbit.author: H. HUTCHLEY
rabbit.platesLine: Illustrated with twelve plates engraved from nature

legal: No rabbit was detained in the making
of this work. One of them hid in it
notice: Of all our wild animals, the wild rabbit is the most common, and perhaps the least understood. Everyone believes they have seen one; very few have looked.
I spent eleven years observing it, in the warrens of my county, at every hour and in all weathers. The present work gathers these observations, with no other ambition than to be accurate.
The plates that accompany it were engraved from nature. The reader will kindly forgive the engraver: the model would not keep still.
noticeMore: I owe, lastly, a word on an observation I did not dare include in the body of the work. One June evening, by a hedge, I saw a white rabbit go by that seemed to be consulting a watch.
I could not follow it: it was in a great hurry, and the hole into which it vanished was too narrow for a man of my age.
I mention it here out of honesty. The naturalists who come after me may be quicker.

chapters.name: Of the rabbit in general
chapters.text: The wild rabbit is a small quadruped of the order of rodents, shorter and stockier than the hare, from which it is told at first glance by its shorter ears and its less sustained running. It lives in colonies, underground, and seldom strays far from where it was born. Its coat is reddish grey on the back, white under the belly and under the tail: it is this white that one sees first, and often only, when it flees.

chapters.name: Of the form and the burrow
chapters.text: Unlike the hare, which is content with a hollow in the grass, the rabbit digs. Its burrow has several galleries, several chambers, and always more than one way out: it never shuts itself in a place from which it could not escape. The observer watching one entrance should know that the animal, at the same moment, is watching another.

chapters.name: Of food
chapters.text: The rabbit feeds on grasses, roots, bark and grain. It prefers wild thyme, clover and young wheat, and does not disdain, on occasion, paper. Country libraries have been visited at night by rabbits, and whole volumes gnawed in the margins, without the text suffering for it.

chapters.name: Of habits and character
chapters.text: The rabbit is timid, but curious. It flees from man, and yet comes back to look at him, from afar, sitting on its haunches, ears upright. It always seems in a hurry, though no one quite knows for what. The old authors call it forgetful; experience proves it remembers very well those who missed it.

chapters.name: Of running and leaping
chapters.text: The rabbit does not run: it bounds. Its flight is a series of leaps, short at first, then longer and longer as it takes fright. It often stops, dead, to listen, and sets off again in a new direction. Chased once, it grows wary; a second time, it doubles its speed; the third time, it is rare that a man catches it.

chapters.name: Of the senses
chapters.text: The ear is the rabbit’s first sense. It turns by itself, this way and that, without the head moving, and catches the slightest rustle of a leaf and, it is said, the sound of a page being turned. The eye, set high and to the side, sees almost all around it, except straight ahead of its nose.

chapters.name: Of the family and the young
chapters.text: The doe gives birth in a separate chamber, which she lines with hay and with the down of her own belly, and whose entrance she stops up each time she leaves. The young are born naked and blind; after three weeks they come out, and from then on come home only on time.

chapters.name: Of the rabbit’s enemies
chapters.text: The fox, the weasel, the ferret, the buzzard, the owl, and man. The rabbit defends itself against none of them; it flees them all, and flight succeeds more often than one would think. The patient hunter takes a few. The hurried hunter takes none.

chapters.name: Of the seasons
chapters.text: In spring, the rabbit is everywhere; in summer, it comes out at dusk; in autumn, it fattens; in winter, it gnaws the bark of young trees and leaves in the snow tracks that one can follow for a long way, up to the spot where they stop for no apparent reason.

chapters.name: Of the tame rabbit
chapters.text: The rabbit is easily raised in a hutch. There it loses its liveliness, gains weight, and takes on colours the warren does not know: black, fawn, pied, and white. The white rabbit with pink eyes is a product of domestication; it is never met with in the wild. Almost never.

chapters.name: Of some singular observations
chapters.text: Every naturalist happens to see what he cannot explain. I report here, without comment, a few facts that have been brought to my attention: a rabbit seen on the same hedge two hours apart, forty leagues away; a burrow whose bottom has never been found; a white rabbit, lastly, which several witnesses saw take a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket, look at it, and hurry on.

chapters.name: Of the manner of observing the rabbit
chapters.text: It requires patience, silence, and a quick hand. The rabbit always shows itself just when one has stopped expecting it. When it appears, one must neither shout nor rise: it is enough to lay a hand on it, without hesitating. He who hesitates will see it again further on, and faster.

pool: Much has been written on the fertility of the rabbit; less has been written on its prudence, which is nevertheless the first of its qualities. Before coming out, it stops at the edge of the hole, its head alone outside, and stays so for a long while, motionless, listening.

The keepers of the forest of *** assured me that rabbits know the step of every man. I could only partly verify it: those of my warren no longer fled from me in the third year, but they fled from my hat.

The colour of the coat varies with the soil. On sandy ground it is paler, on heavy ground darker, so that the motionless animal blends with the earth, and is often discovered only at the moment it bolts.

The rabbit strikes the ground with its hind feet to warn its fellows of danger. This dull sound, heard from very far on calm evenings, at once sends the whole warren home, and the observer is left alone before empty holes.

I have measured, on loose soil, leaps of more than two metres. The fleeing animal lengthens its bounds as it gets further away, and the gap between the prints tells, better than any witness, whether it was afraid or playing.

The young play together at dusk, at the mouth of the burrows: they chase one another, leap over each other and hide behind the smallest tuft of grass, with an agility that discourages the draughtsman.
One cannot recommend too strongly that the observer note the hour of each appearance. The rabbit has its habits, and whoever knows them can tell, to within a few minutes, where he will see it pass.
One must not trust the rabbit’s stillness. The animal that seems asleep, eyes half closed, in the sun, has already counted your steps, and chosen the hole through which it will disappear.

hunt.say: “Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be too late!”
hunt.home: The rabbit goes back to his plates.

idleBabel.name: Idle Babel
idleBabel.subtitle: From its design to its making

forewordText: Every library ends up holding the book of its own making. This one is no exception.
This book tells how Idle Babel was made, by two hands: someone who imagined, and a machine that wrote the code. It does not tell everything. It tells what was kept.
The chapters follow the stages of its making. The plates show the bindings as they were drawn before they entered the game, and the drafts that were set aside.
This book is not finished. Neither is the game.
pages.plateNote: front and spine, after the mock-up
colophon: This book is still being written.
It will grow with the game.

idea.title: The idea
text: Before it was a game, Idle Babel was words.
First, a story by Borges: a library made of hexagons, holding every possible book of four hundred and ten pages. Nearly all of them mean nothing. Somewhere, though, this one is already written.
Then a question. What if someone were alone in there, reading without end? A game where you do almost nothing, where pages turn while you look away. An idle.

The foundations were set down in writing: a seeker, a room, pages read, a Knowledge born by chance out of the gibberish. Then numbers: what each thing costs, how long one must wait. They were put to the test before a single line of code, so that the waiting would be fair.
The first name was longer. It was shortened.
The ending was written then too, before everything else. It will not be told here.

demo.title: Tech demo and trials
text: Then came the trying. Finding out whether the words would stand once they became image, light, paper. A tech demo: build, take apart, build again.

reading.head: Reading
text: In the beginning there was only a page that said hello in two languages. Then a room was painted: a window, shelves, a cellar light. The light was put out. The room only brightens as you read.
A book came into the seeker’s hands. Its page lifts, curls, falls back; you can hold it at the tip of the mouse, and hesitate. Then the pages learned to turn on their own, at the pace of production.

firstBooks.head: The first books
text: The books were given their true length, four hundred and ten pages. At the end they close, and the next one wears another binding: a gilt title in Babel’s symbols, a frame, a fleuron, leather more or less worn. Now and then a title means something. Do not trust it too much.

strangeBook.head: The strange book
text: A great book, waiting to be found, that counts everything you do. It cannot be read at once: it must be deciphered, page after page, all the way to its title. Later, it began to speak.

exerciseBook.head: The exercise book
text: The settings were first a sketchbook, then a school exercise book. On its back, every multiplication makes four hundred and ten. There is a secret there; this book will not say which.

seals.head: The seals
text: A seal for each thing done, announced by a vision. Some are secret. For each one, a sentence somewhere tells how to find it.

knowledge.head: Knowledge and the white book
text: In the gibberish, now and then, something looks like a word. That is Knowledge. A white book keeps everything you find: reading methods, memories, sentences.

depth.head: Depth
text: Everything moved into three dimensions. The book held in your hands got a wider cover, rounded pages, a top dipping towards the fold. The right curve took a long time to find. The books read piled up nearby.

voice.head: The voice
text: The game learned to ask the name of whoever comes in, and to tell memories: the waking, “Nowhere”, then the white book speaking in its own words.

numerals.head: Babel’s numerals
text: The Library was given numerals of its own: a gilt hexagon and rays you count around it. Large numbers can be written as you please, even spelled out.

anomalies.head: The anomalies
text: Then the books began to answer. Famous quotations slipped into chance, sentences about the staircase and the mirror, others that speak to the reader. This book will not say which.

rareBooks.head: Rare books
text: One book in two hundred is not like the others: a rare book, with a real title and a seal of its own. A black notebook where names get written, a directory where someone already holds your place, an essay on the blank page signed by an author who does not exist.
Later, a sports almanac, straight off an eighties newsstand: fifty years of results, already written.

Then the Necronomicon, the book Lovecraft made up, which the Library is bound to hold: the Arabic original, Al Azif, bound in morocco, a gold medallion full of signs that cannot be read. Inside, a manuscript in a script no one reads; only a reader who came before left Lovecraft’s line in pencil.

Then Dad Jokes, a humour book of the kind people give on Father’s Day: bright yellow, glasses, a moustache, a question you have heard before. It takes the place of a Book of the Dead, planned at first. Inside, four hundred and seven jokes. There are only ninety: they keep coming back.

Then the Voynich Manuscript, the one book no one has ever been able to read. On its vellum cover grows a plant that does not exist. Inside, more plants, circles of stars, pools, apothecary jars, and an unknown script, drawn stroke by stroke.

Then the Catalogue of Catalogues, the one Borges’s librarians search for. On its midnight-blue leather cover, the book contains itself, until it is nothing but a point of gold. Inside, a register of books, one per line, each with its shelf mark.

Then the Book of Sand, from a story by Borges, with neither a first page nor a last. On its cover, a desert at dusk, and the word “Sand” blowing away grain by grain. Inside, endless verses, page numbers that follow no order, and not one page you can find again.

Then the Big Book of X, which tells the story of the letter X, from the caves to the Library. On its cream cover, a huge black X, like a type specimen. Inside, each chapter begins with a short story, and the rest is written in the X language.

Then they became harder to find: all of them could be had in a few hours. Each rare book found makes the next one a quarter rarer. The first comes quickly; the last, one book in forty-two thousand, takes hundreds of hours. They belong to no age: a very long-term reward. The Ledger gave them a chapter, “Rarities”: how many have been found, and, as a percentage, the chance that the next book is one. How many are left, it does not say; when none are left, a line says so.

Then Dark Patterns by Example, a bestseller of today for interface designers, with a foreword of the utmost seriousness. In the library, its examples are not read: they are endured. A cookie banner, a button that runs away, a countdown, an endless unsubscribe, a forced subscription, a basket that fills itself, disguised ads, an invented crowd, double-negative boxes, a feed that never ends: you have to find the way out. There is always one.

Then The Wild Rabbit, a natural history treatise from the century before, in green cloth and gold. On its cover, an engraved medallion: the grass, the hedge, the burrow, and the rabbit’s place, empty. Inside, twelve plates he is always missing from. That is because he runs: in the library, Alice’s White Rabbit sometimes bounds across the pages. He has to be caught three times; each time, he comes back faster.

library.head: The library
text: To keep them, an old wooden showcase, a brass light in every box, and a small key leaning against the pile. The first book you finish goes in first.

classics.head: The classics
text: Then the classics came. Alice in her red cloth, Moby-Dick in embossed slate, a family Bible, the Arabian Nights in burgundy morocco, the Odyssey under pebbled paper, Don Quixote in the red cloth of the great Doré edition, with the title page of Madrid, 1605, as a flyleaf, the Divine Comedy in midnight-blue morocco with the whole universe of the poem tooled in gold, Hell, Purgatory and the nine heavens, the Manuscript Found in Saragossa in the tree calf of its 1814 edition, which ends on the promise of a sequel that never came, and blank pages, the Encyclopédie of Diderot and d’Alembert in the mottled calf of its subscribers, the Preliminary Discourse, then, in two columns, the articles that speak of the Library: Babel, Library, Book. Public domain texts, set line by line, in small pieces, so that the game would not run out of breath.
Every book was given a silk ribbon that hangs and sways. The first one cracked like a whip. The second was calmer.

credits.head: The credits
text: The credits were written: who made the game, with what, after what. Later, at the foot of the screen, the build date gave way to the version’s name, “Version Alpha 1”: a click opens the credits on their update notes. The first ones are written there: those of Alpha 1.

seed.head: The seed
text: Every game got its seed: a hidden number that the covers, the pages, the rare books and the finds are drawn from. Same seed, same Library. Only the options notebook writes it down, so it can be handed over if something goes wrong.

ledger.head: The Ledger
text: The strange book was given a name: the Ledger, where the accounts are kept. Nobody pays to read it any more: each part clears up on its own once Knowledge has grown enough, and a golden star says so. When it comes to hand, a short story announces it, then it opens wide. Later, its seal plates were evened out: a page only moves on to the next once its five rows are full.

bindings.head: The bindings
text: The ordinary books got their details. Leather with a grain, gilt tools in the corners, a roll around the frame, and gold that wears away with the leather. One book in four is half-bound: leather on the spine and corners, marbled paper on the boards.

On the spine, raised bands, a title label, sometimes a volume number, and the shelf mark sticker. The edges took on colours: sprinkled, red, yellow, gilt, marbled. Inside, marbled endpapers and the Library’s bookplate.
Among the modern books, two new kinds: autobiographies, where the faces stay blank, and comics, numbered like a series.

away.head: Absence
text: The game learned to go on without the player. Game closed or tab hidden, pages are read at the pace of production, at half rate, eight hours at most. The book in hand moves on, finished books close, rare books met along the way are found, seals follow.
On return, the seeker thinks they are waking from a dream. A modal sets them straight, and tells what their hands did without them.

With the white book or the library open, the book in hand is gone: for a long time its pages stopped turning, and nothing was found in them. Back to the game, that time now counts like an open window. And pages turning on their own never went past ten leaves a second, whatever their cap: now they keep it.

intuitions.head: Intuitions
text: Knowledge found a use. The white book got one more part, right after the methods: intuitions, things the seeker senses before understanding them.

The first is the semantic filter. Five levels, paid in Knowledge, and with each one finds come more often. Its page says it all: the level, the chance before and after, the price in pencil. A first attempt, notes in the margin, could not be understood. It was redone.

Then the others came: Ariadne’s thread, the memory of sentences, speed reading, muscle memory, the map of the return, flair, and one per reading method, which doubles what the method reads. The one for a method not yet found stays in symbols. Only one has no end: deep sleep, one more hour of absence counted at each level, each twice as dear. Then a second one without end, economy of gesture: methods cost a little less at each level. And because intuitions will be forgotten at the Exile, reminiscence is ready: they come back on their own up to the highest level already reached, and a pencil note lets it happen or not. It became a lasting intuition, which only appears after the first Exile.

Knowledge came too fast. Finds became rarer, prices higher: it now takes hundreds of hours to understand everything. In the white book and the hive of methods, each method shows what it really reads, intuition included. Under the hive, a gold mark tells how many a click buys: one, ten, a hundred, or as many as the pages allow. It unfolds when the mouse passes over it. Each lot opens with the armful, the first of the lasting intuitions: a comfort that the Exile will not take away. The Ledger got one more plate, “Intuitions”: a seal for each one understood to the end; for those with no end, at level ten. Each seal also makes finds more frequent, by one percent, and the chance can go beyond a hundred percent: at 554%, a page brings five finds, and a sixth at 54%. Only one is shown highlighted.

Then the first age slowed down. A method can only be found once the one before is owned twenty-five times; until then, pencil tally marks count them under its name, in fives. The last five cost twice as much: the ladder comes around the fourteenth hour. Beyond a hundred percent, the extra finds bring their Knowledge but write almost nothing: a little method, a little hint, a little memory. And a hint that leads to a rare book waits until that book is found.

Then the first age lost four methods: the thumb, the wide gaze, the double leafing and the mirror. Five per age, no more, so that each one counts. The prices were redone, and the ladder still comes around the fourteenth hour. A game that had them has forgotten them. Each method received its seals: one, twenty-five, fifty, a hundred, a hundred and fifty and five hundred copies, in a single game. Five hundred ladders cost a number of pages thirty-nine digits long: the last ones are meant for very long games. In the Great Book, each method now has its own page, its name as a subtitle, and a second series: the pages it has read since waking, from ten times its price to a trillion times. A last page gathers them all: every method bought in the game fills a volume of four hundred and ten, like the pages of a book of the Library. Nine volumes, nine seals. The “Pages” plate got a second page, for what is never forgotten, even when starting over: the pages read by the methods, a thousand at a time, from a single one to a number thirty-one digits long; and those read by hand, ten at a time, up to a hundred thousand. Each of these seals has its own sentence, its numbers written the way the player chose in the notebook. A third page follows, for the highest speed of a whole life: ten times more pages per second each time up to a hundred million, then a hundred times more, up to a number thirty-one digits long.

prestige.head: Prestige
text: After a billion pages, a violet book lands on the pile, glowing. The seeker opens it, and the floor gives way. When he opens his eyes again, the book is in his hand: the Etherium. The story is told only once: the times after, a short question only says what will be lost.

Everything he held is lost: pages, methods, Knowledge, intuitions, and the methods’ sentences, which the white book forgets. What remains: the pages read in all, the seals, the rare books and the rest of the white book. They are worth Ether: the cube root of the pages, in billions. It is spent in the Etherium, one page per tree, a stem gilded node after node: reading, hands, Knowledge, finds, head start, memory of methods. Once closed, the book disappears. A dream? Diagonal Reading, though, comes back on the very first page.

Then the Etherium’s cover was redone. At first, a violet book, bare. At a million pages read, its name appears, and a hive. A cell lights up for each digit of the Ether the prestige would bring; the next one fills towards the following power of ten. Before the first Ether, the middle one fills, its percentage written inside. The exact number is written below, the way the player chose; on the back, the Ether in reserve. The hive had to hold numbers sixty digits long. The Great Book got a chapter, “Ether”, after the first prestige: the Ether in reserve and what was poured into the Etherium, the Ether received in all, what a prestige would bring, and the pages still missing before the next one. Later, the “Hours” chapter also told how many times the researcher had opened their eyes again.

Then the Etherium came to the pile from the very start, a violet book that feeds on the pages read. It is taken in hand like the others, its cover and its back looked at; opening its cover is the prestige. Until that brings one Ether, the cover resists: it barely lifts and falls back. Then it glows. Each time, a short question says what will be lost and the Ether gained; “Open” must be clicked. The first time only, the floor gives way, and when the seeker opens his eyes again, nothing is left around him: the book has fed on everything. Put back, it no longer disappears: it goes back to the pile, sealed until the next prestige.

constellations.head: The constellations
text: Then the Etherium turned to night. Its single-stemmed trees were meant to branch; three ideas were drawn: the fork, the tree of Porphyry, the double page. None was kept. Instead, one invented constellation per page, its figure telling what it gives: an open book for reading, a hand, an owl for Knowledge, a magnifying glass for finds, a moon for absence, a door for waking, a hive for the memory of methods, a staircase for the Ages. Each star has only one star before it; it is lit with Ether, and what the stars give multiplies. The nodes of the old trees gave back their Ether. Then, one by one, the stars were given what they promised: leaves that turn faster, cheaper intuitions, a door that remembers the run before.

For the ink, four nights were tried: the atlas on paper, the night, the restrained night, the night that is earned. Plain night won: violet pages, a fixed dust of stars, gold lines that shine. In the room, the lamp turned it maroon; its pages were given what they need to keep their violet.

Then Ether began to count even once spent: every Ether ever received makes reading one percent faster, for methods and hands alike. The flyleaf says so beneath the Ether to spend, the return from an absence tells the Ether it earned, and the Ledger breaks reading speed down as it does the chance of a find: the methods, their intuitions, the Etherium, the Ether. The list of methods got pages of its own there, sorted by Age once the Automatic Age is bought: there will be dozens. Not enough to get past the wall: enough to make it lower.

Before the Alpha, a review of the whole game. The simulator learned the seals and the Ether that makes reading faster: in a month, the whole Etherium lights up; the next Ages will have their constellations, far dearer. Until then, their steps stay closed, like the Drop in the Hive: one sees them, without their name. The find chance got its share of the Etherium, and a few words were set straight. With the Etherium open, its cover lifted, the counter at the top shows the Ether to spend instead of pages: one could no longer tell how much was left.

cornee.head: The Dog-Eared Page
text: The first star of the Hive was given its method: the Dog-Eared Page, the secret method of the Manual Age. Once lit, it brings back a blurred memory: a page of the white book in symbols, a sentence to find alongside the current method. Once found, it is never forgotten, not even at prestige. It took the last place, after the Ladder.

automaticAge.head: The Automatic Age
text: A step of the Staircase was given its Age: the Automatic Age, for one star of Ether. Bought once and for all, it opens five mechanisms that read for the researcher, from the smallest to the whole gallery: the Metronome, the Book Wheel, the Book Lift, the Reading Automaton and the Gallery Clock. Each has its sentence, its intuition and its seals. The first one does not wait for twenty-five Ladders: buying the Age is enough. Their prices were chosen with the simulator, out of four attempts. In the white book, methods and intuitions are then sorted by Age, each under its own title.

sealsReview.head: The seals catch up with the game
text: Prestige, the Etherium and the Automatic Age had arrived without a single seal. A review caught up with them: a plate for the Etherium, which only appears after a first awakening (prestiges, Ether gathered, stars lit, each whole constellation, the Automatic Age); knowledge understood, the white book filled, the Great Book read whole, a whole night away, the days since arriving. The seals of a method no longer show before it does: nothing of the Dog-Eared Page or the Automatic Age before they exist for the researcher. Series that were too short were extended to the numbers the game now reaches, and the pages turned by hand were given nine more sentences, up to the empty hand of the first day. Three secrets were added, each with its sentence in the white book; a solved hint carries in its margin, in gold, the seal it earned.

We were told that seals appeared without anyone knowing what they stood for. The vision now writes beneath the seal the name of its plate and its caption, in Babel symbols while the seals cannot be read yet, with a line that admits it; it waits while hovered, and a click opens the Great Book on its plate, where the seal waits, highlighted, its caption already written. The first seals fall before the Great Book and cannot be touched: the first three visions that can be touched say so. Three options were tried.

letter.head: The letter that escapes
text: After the Alpha, an idea from the author: boons that do not last. Four things were tried to carry them: a page flying off a shelf, a golden moth, a letter escaping the book, a book spine that glows. The letter won. From time to time, a letter of Babel rises from the book in hand; caught, it comes apart in golden dust and gives a boon, for a few seconds. What is running shows in a medallion, right of the counter, ringed with the time left.

At first it is rare, brief, and gives only the Trance. A ninth constellation, the Quill, makes it come more often, stay longer, and teaches it six other boons: the Sharp Eye, the Light Hand, the Quick Memory, the Windfall, the Flash, the Find. The prices were raised: in the long run, it is a very strong boon. From the first letter caught, three intuitions appear: the Watch, the Held Breath, the Letter Understood. And, very rarely, it is not a letter that comes but a word, letter by letter: BABEL. The white book, for its part, set apart the intuitions that belong to no method: once the Ages are separated, they have their own sub-part, before them.

thisBook.head: This book
text: Then this book was bound: morocco, the plan of a gallery tooled in gold. The Library must hold the book of its own making. Someone had to write it.
This is where the game stands. It is still being tried.
